Suan Pan in Various Number Systems

Place ValueCountingArithmetic
Game: A Chinese counting frame. Beads touching the middle bar count: ones below, fives above. Five ones turn into a five, and two fives into one on the next wire.
How to play: Click a bead to slide it. Watch the frame tidy up after you. Choose another radix to count in other number systems.
Look for the math

The suan pan is the Chinese abacus. A bar splits it into heaven and earth. Every wire has five earth beads worth one each and two heaven beads worth five each. A bead counts when it touches the bar.

More beads than digits need

Four ones and one five already make every digit from 0 to 9, as on the Japanese soroban. The suan pan's extra earth bead and extra heaven bead let a wire hold up to 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. The same layout works in any even base r, with r/2 earth beads and heaven beads worth r/2, so a wire can hold up to 3r/2. Some values can then be shown in two ways (five ones, or one five), and the logic test checked that every value from 0 to 3r/2 occurs, for every base from 2 to 20.

Trading and carrying

The applet tidies up after you, as an abacus user would. Five ones become one five. Two fives become one bead on the next wire to the left, the carry, because that wire is worth r times as much. Trades never change the number on the frame, except that a carry from the leftmost wire has nowhere to go. The test tried 16,000 clicks in every base and found the number kept every time.

Three repairs

The original applet could lose value while tidying. A wire that had once traded five ones would later put a five back instead of carrying. A carry also cleared the wire's ones. And a carry on any wire but the rightmost busy one could be dropped. This page makes the same trades in the same order, without those slips.

Make 9 on the units wire, then push one more earth bead up and watch the 10 ripple along.
